tldr: By integrating a physics-based three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT) into a reinforcement learning simulator, foot sinking and lateral slip are accurately captured. This enables a humanoid control system that can walk and run agilely across diverse granular terrains, such as beach sand and basalt gravel.
hero_caption: The walking and running policies deployed on the real robot across diverse real-world granular terrains (from left: basalt gravel, dry sand, and beach sand). Even on harsh sand where foot penetration and large slip occur, the robot moves forward without losing its posture.
overview:
Granular ground such as sandy beaches or gravel paths exhibits complex behavior, acting like a solid under load or flowing like a fluid when yielding. Conventional robotics has typically either assumed the ground to be an unyielding "rigid body" or applied simplified normal force models while awkwardly tacking on heuristic friction laws for horizontal forces. However, this fails to capture the realistic physical phenomenon of feet sinking into sand while slipping sideways. As a result, walking policies trained in simulation would quickly stumble and fall when transferred to real-world sand.

To solve this, the research team focused on three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT), which can resolve granular penetration dynamics accurately and rapidly. They built a GPU-based contact simulator that places differential contact elements across the humanoid's sole, calculates 3D resistive forces from each element's depth, velocity vector, and surface orientation, and feeds them back into the robot's whole-body dynamics as a resultant wrench. Furthermore, to handle variations in sand stiffness that cannot be identified visually, they introduced a teacher-student reinforcement learning pipeline. Here, privileged terrain parameters are compressed into a latent representation via a variational autoencoder (VAE), and a student policy estimates this latent variable solely from the robot's joint and IMU sensor history.

After validating the contact model's physical fidelity and the policy's robustness using high-precision continuum simulations (material point method, MPM), the team deployed the system on a full-sized humanoid, the Unitree G1. While a policy trained on a conventional rigid-body model fell immediately at speeds above 1.5 m/s on dry sand, the proposed method achieved stable running up to 2.5 m/s. Furthermore, when the ground suddenly turned soft during walking, the robot instantly inferred sand stiffness from underfoot sensations and naturally exhibited an adaptive behavior, lifting its swing leg higher to avoid dragging its toes.
contributions: Integrated a physically consistent granular contact model based on three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT) into an RL simulation environment, eliminating empirical assumptions and ad-hoc friction heuristics.

Constructed a terrain-adaptive control framework via teacher-student RL using a VAE that explicitly reconstructs terrain stiffness parameters, adjusting foot clearance and gait using only proprioception.

Demonstrated agile humanoid locomotion up to 2.5 m/s and real-time terrain adaptation on a full-sized humanoid across diverse real-world environments—basalt gravel, dry sand, and beach sand—for the first time.

sections.heading: Why is bipedal walking on sand so difficult?
sections.summary: Granular terrains like sand and gravel exhibit both solid- and fluid-like behaviors, generating strong nonlinear forces underfoot that make control extremely difficult. This study introduces physics-based 3D resistive force theory into reinforcement learning to achieve agile humanoid locomotion on unseen sandy terrains without falling.
sections.details:
To make robots useful in the real world, the ability to walk on deformable ground (granular terrain) like sandy beaches and unpaved roads is essential. However, granular media change their stiffness and fluidity under load, causing feet to sink deeply and slip unexpectedly. This makes balance control for bipedal robots exceptionally difficult.

Traditional model-based methods incorporated simplified penetration dynamics into trajectory optimization. However, they relied on predefined contact sequences, could not handle large outdoor disturbances, and remained confined to small robots in laboratory settings. On the other hand, recent deep reinforcement learning (RL) can acquire robust locomotion, but most work either assumes a "rigid ground" and glosses over issues using domain randomization (randomly jittering parameters), or applies a simplified model only for normal forces while tacking on Coulomb friction horizontally. This fails to accurately capture the distinctive three-dimensional resistance of sand.

The key here is to use a single, physically principled 3D model. In this paper, the authors introduce experimentally validated three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT) into the simulator. They also propose a learning pipeline that estimates sand stiffness from proprioception to automatically adjust the gait.

sections.heading: The evolution of granular simulation and locomotion learning
sections.summary: Prior work is organized from three perspectives: granular contact mechanics, legged locomotion on deformable ground, and terrain-adaptive control. Because high-fidelity particle simulations are too computationally heavy for learning, this work couples an analytical RFT-based approach with large-scale parallel reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
### II-A Granular Contact Modeling
Modeling the interaction between a robot's foot and sand has long been a challenge. Major physics engines assume "non-penetration" during contact, so they cannot represent foot sinking into sand. Meanwhile, the discrete element method (DEM), which simulates individual sand grains, and the material point method (MPM), which solves continuum equations on a grid, offer extremely high physical fidelity. However, they are far too computationally expensive for RL running thousands of robots in parallel. Simplified models like spring-dampers ignore the fluid-like behavior of sand. Therefore, this study adopts resistive force theory (RFT), which is computationally lightweight yet closely matches MPM and experimental data.

### II-B Legged Robots on Deformable Terrain
Model-based approaches have attempted hopping and walking on mud or sand, but they were vulnerable to modeling errors and had limited practicality. In RL approaches, some studies combined vertical RFT with Coulomb friction for quadrupeds, or tackled bipedal walking on mattresses, but horizontal resistance relied on ad-hoc designs. This work integrates fully physics-derived 3D RFT into the mainstream simulator IsaacLab to tackle humanoid running and jumping.

### II-C Terrain-Adaptive Locomotion
Teacher-student RL is widely used to adjust foot clearance and cadence according to terrain stiffness and unevenness. Most prior works trained the latent space using only policy gradients. In contrast, this study uses a variational autoencoder (VAE) tasked with explicitly reconstructing the sand stiffness parameter itself, obtaining a robust representation with clear physical meaning.

sections.heading: Incorporating 3D resistive force theory into whole-body dynamics
sections.summary: This section explains the formulation of 3D RFT, which computes three-dimensional resistive forces for each grid element on the sole from penetration depth, velocity direction, and surface orientation. Aggregating these into a resultant wrench around the ankle and feeding it into the whole-body equations of motion reproduces accurate contact behavior while keeping computational cost low.
sections.details:
When an object penetrates granular media like sand, the force per unit area and depth $\bm{\alpha}$ is determined by the geometric relationship among velocity direction $\mathbf{e}_v$, surface normal $\mathbf{e}_n$, and gravity direction $\mathbf{e}_g$. In this work, resistive force functions $\mathbf{G}$ at arbitrary 3D intrusion angles are calculated using cubic polynomial functions derived from experiments and MPM simulations.

The total contact force $\mathbf{F}$ acting on the foot is expressed as an area integral over the differential sole elements submerged below the terrain surface. Specifically, it is computed as:
$$\mathbf{F} = \int_{S} \bm{\alpha} |z| \mathds{1}_{z<0} \mathrm{d}S$$
Here, $z$ is the height relative to the terrain surface (negative when penetrated), and $\mathds{1}_{z<0}$ is an indicator function that equals 1 only during penetration. The force $\bm{\alpha}$ is scaled by a factor $\xi = \rho_c g f(\tilde{\mu})$, which reflects material density $\rho_c$ and internal friction coefficient $\tilde{\mu}$.

A clever implementation detail is how this is passed into the robot's equations of motion (whole-body dynamics). Treating every sole element as an individual contact point, as done in prior work, blows up the Jacobian size and slows down simulation speed. Instead, this method aggregates the forces and moments computed across the grid points on the sole into a single wrench (resultant force and torque pair) at the ankle position and feeds it directly into the ankle joint. This drastically cuts computational overhead.

captions.F2: Definition of the contact model based on three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT). For each differential element on the sole, the local resistive force $\mathbf{F}_i$ is obtained from penetration depth $z_i$, velocity vector angle $\gamma$, surface orientation $\beta$, and twist angle $\psi$. These are aggregated into the total contact force $\mathbf{F}$ and moment $\mathbf{M}$ around the ankle joint $\mathbf{p}_b$.

sections.heading: A two-stage learning framework that senses sand stiffness and adapts gait
sections.summary: A teacher policy with privileged information and a VAE terrain encoder are trained simultaneously, then distilled into a student policy that infers the terrain's latent representation solely from proprioceptive history available on the real robot. Having the VAE reconstruct only the sand stiffness scaling factor extracts features directly tied to locomotion adaptation.
sections.details:
### IV-A Terrain-Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
Sand stiffness in the real world varies widely across locations. For stable walking, a robot must adjust foot clearance and pitch in real time based on the stiffness underfoot. However, ground stiffness cannot be directly measured as a numerical value from cameras or tactile sensors. Therefore, this study adopts a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework.

In the first stage (teacher training), asymmetric actor-critic is used. The critic and the "teacher terrain encoder" receive privileged information available only in simulation (accurate contact forces underfoot, absolute foot height, terrain material scaling factor $\eta$, etc.). This encoder is structured as a VAE, outputting latent variables $\mathbf{z}_t$ from privileged information and proprioceptive history. Importantly, instead of having the decoder reconstruct the entire full-body state, it is tasked with reconstructing only the normalized terrain scaling factor $\eta = \xi/\xi_{\text{max}}$. This forces the latent space to specialize in "terrain stiffness."

In the second stage (student training), a "student terrain encoder" is trained without any privileged information, taking only proprioceptive history over the past $N$ steps (joint positions, velocities, IMU readings, etc.) as input. Alongside a distillation loss to mimic the teacher's actions, a representation matching loss is applied so that the encoder's latent variables and decoded output match the teacher. This imbues the student with the ability to infer sand stiffness from the history of foot vibrations and resistance.

### IV-B Environment Design and Training Details
The action space consists of position command offsets for all 29 whole-body joints from a nominal pose. To accelerate parallel simulation, a soft-terrain contact solver running on the GPU was implemented using NVIDIA Warp. This allows 4,096 agents to run simultaneously on a single RTX 4090 GPU, progressing RL training at ultra-high speeds of hundreds of thousands of FPS.

Additionally, rather than starting on soft sand right away, a "terrain curriculum" is introduced where the robot first trains on stiff ground and gradually faces softer, sinking sand as success rates improve. This prevents training from destabilizing.

captions.F3: Overall system architecture of the proposed terrain-adaptive humanoid locomotion control. The teacher network on the left compresses sand stiffness from privileged information using a VAE. The student network on the right reconstructs those latent variables from temporal proprioceptive history ($o_{t-N:t}$) available on the real robot to output joint commands.

sections.heading: Remarkable traversal capabilities shown in simulation and on hardware
sections.summary: After confirming the physical consistency of 3D RFT using high-fidelity MPM simulations, real-robot running experiments were conducted on the full-sized humanoid G1. The proposed method achieved high-speed running at 2.5 m/s and demonstrated adaptive behavior that autonomously increases foot clearance when ground stiffness changes.
sections.details:
### V-A Simulation Evaluation
First is the evaluation of the contact model itself. A 35 kg cuboid matching the humanoid's mass was launched into sand at an initial velocity of 1.0 m/s. Its horizontal travel distance, penetration depth, and ground reaction forces (GRF) were compared against high-fidelity continuum simulations (MPM). Conventional simplified models (such as Heuristic-RFT) had zero lateral reaction forces and slipped excessively in the horizontal direction. In contrast, the proposed 3D-RFT neatly reproduced MPM behavior, including lateral drag forces.

Next, locomotion policies trained with each contact model were tested in an MPM environment (extremely soft sand modeled after poppy seeds). Under harsh conditions such as turning gaits and 30 cm deep sand, policies trained on conventional models could not withstand lateral slip and repeatedly fell. Policies trained on 3D-RFT achieved a significantly higher success rate. Furthermore, when applied to imitation learning of jumping motions, the rigid model slipped during takeoff and failed, whereas 3D-RFT succeeded in impressive jumping and landing on sand.

### V-B Hardware Experiments
The trained policy was directly deployed on the Unitree G1 (about 130 cm tall, about 35 kg) and tested across three types of sandy terrain: basalt gravel, dry sand on a volleyball court, and a real beach.

When forward velocity commands were gradually increased from 0.5 m/s on dry sand, the policy trained on rigid ground (Rigid) could not withstand foot-sinking disturbances and fell above 1.5 m/s. In contrast, the proposed method (Ours) ran stably up to the maximum speed of 2.5 m/s, with minimal tracking error against commanded velocity. On basalt terrain mixed with coarse gravel, Rigid fell immediately at all speeds, while the proposed method completed walking and running across the entire velocity range.

Analyzing ankle pitch torque from motor currents on the hardware revealed that the proposed method kept peak torque substantially lower than the baseline. This confirms that the robot uses its ankles compliantly based on estimated terrain stiffness, absorbing impact without kicking sand away unnecessarily.

### V-C Real-Time Adaptation to Terrain Transitions
An experiment was conducted walking from hard ground into a soft sand mound. The moment the proposed robot stepped onto the sand mound, it rapidly decreased its estimated stiffness $\eta$ from underfoot sensations. In tandem, it automatically raised swing foot clearance from the normal ~9 cm up to 16 cm. In contrast, a standard PPO policy lacking adaptive capabilities dragged its toes in the sand, lost balance, and triggered large torque spikes.

captions.F5: Scatter plot of horizontal travel distance and penetration depth (left) and temporal profile of ground reaction forces (right) when launching a 35 kg object. The proposed 3D-RFT (blue) accurately matches both the distribution and the three-axis force profiles of the MPM baseline (dark blue).
captions.F10: Online terrain adaptation results when stepping into a sand mound on the real robot. The proposed method (Ours) instantly detects decreased stiffness upon entering the soft region and raises foot clearance to walk smoothly, whereas the baseline (PPO) drags its feet and causes large torque spikes.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: By combining fast, high-fidelity granular contact modeling via 3D RFT with VAE-based terrain-adaptive learning, this work realizes agile humanoid locomotion on real-world sand. Future directions include extending to slopes and uneven terrains, as well as exploring more energy-efficient sand locomotion gaits.
sections.details:
This paper breaks through the long-standing barrier of "agile humanoid locomotion on real-world granular terrain." At the core of this achievement are the integration of 3D RFT—which physically solves 3D forces without heuristic friction rules—into the simulator, and a teacher-student learning framework that reads sand stiffness from proprioception to instantly adjust foot lifting.

The authors highlight future work such as handling complex geometries like slopes and undulating sand dunes, as well as optimizing long-distance locomotion patterns to minimize energy consumption on sand. This research marks a major step toward bipedal robots operating like humans in outdoor, unstructured environments.

takeaways: Blindly applying domain randomization has limits; embedding the core contact physics of sinking and lateral slip (3D RFT) into the simulator is key to Sim-to-Real success.
Aggregating forces across sole elements into a single wrench at the ankle maintains physical accuracy while preserving the computational speed needed for GPU-parallel reinforcement learning.

In teacher-student learning, restricting the VAE's reconstruction target strictly to the "terrain stiffness coefficient" allows the policy to accurately extract only the terrain features essential for control from proprioception.
limitations: The evaluated terrains were essentially flat sand or sand mounds; adapting to geometric irregularities such as steep sand slopes or undulating dunes remains future work.
Because the entire sole is modeled as a rigid plate, fine-scale phenomena such as elastic deformation of the real robot's rubber sole or tread pattern interlocking are not accounted for.
Locomotion is not yet optimized for energy consumption, leaving room for debate on how efficiently the robot can traverse long distances on sand.
